BIOGUARD

A small six-wheeled rover that helps a burned hillside keep its soil. It spreads mulch, plants native seed and lays mini wattles, then checks its own work.

Chapter 1

After a wildfire, the hill can't hold on

1

Fire burns the plants. Their roots used to hold the soil together like a net. Now the ground is bare and covered in ash.

2

Rain hits bare soil. Nothing slows the water down. It runs downhill fast and carries soil with it.

3

The soil is gone. Muddy water fills streams, and new plants have nothing to grow in. Crews can't reach every steep slope by hand.

When a hill burns, there are no roots left to hold the dirt. The next rain washes it away. BIOGUARD covers and protects the soil before that happens.

A picture of the idea, not measured data.
Chapter 2

Three treatments in one trip

Crews already use these three on burned slopes. BIOGUARD does all three at once, in neat lanes, without anyone climbing the hill.

Mulch

A blanket for the soil

Wood mulch soaks up raindrops so they don't smash the soil loose, and keeps the ground damp for seeds.

Native seed

New roots, new net

Seeds of local plants sprout under the mulch. Their roots grow into a new net that holds the soil for years.

Mini wattle

A speed bump for water

A wattle is a roll of straw laid across the slope. Water slows down behind it and drops the soil it was carrying.

Our robot does three things in one trip. Mulch is a blanket, seeds grow roots, and wattles are speed bumps for water.

Chapter 4

Sense → think → act

Every robot does the same three things. Sensors notice the world, the Arduino decides, and motors move. BIOGUARD repeats this loop many times a second.

The sensors are the robot's eyes and balance. The Arduino is the brain: it runs our program. The motors are its muscles. If something is wrong, like tipping or a rock ahead, the brain stops the muscles.

Chapter 5

How we test it: the rain test

A fair test changes one thing only. We build two identical slopes, treat one with BIOGUARD, and leave the other bare. Then we rain on both.

1 · Same rain1 litre from a watering can, from the same height, on each tray.
2 · Catch the runoffClear cups at the bottom. Let the mud settle.
3 · Dry and weighDry the mud and weigh it. Less mud means the soil stayed on the hill.
4 · Repeat 3 timesOne test can be luck. Three tests show a pattern.
